title: Enabling U.S. Foreign Investment in South Asia
text:
Enabling U.S. Foreign Investment in South Asia

Photo by Wong Yu Liang via Getty Images

November 18th, 2026

Executive SummarySouth Asia remains underrepresented in U.S. foreign investment positions relative to its demographic, economic, and strategic scale. Within the region, the distribution of U.S. capital is also uneven. India has attracted substantially greater U.S. direct and portfolio investments over the past decade, while positions in Pakistan and Bangladesh have remained considerably smaller.The divergence in U.S. investments in India compared to its neighbors points to differences in the conditions that enable foreign investment. There are three enabling factors for foreign investment in which India has made greater progress relative to its regional peers: economic formalization and digitization, capital-market depth and accessibility, and diaspora networks. Formalization and digitization can improve the visibility of firms and transactions, reduce administrative and compliance frictions, and expand access to finance and reliable commercial information. Deeper and more accessible capital markets provide foreign portfolio investors with greater liquidity, scale, and investable securities. Diaspora networks can reduce barriers to information and market-entry by connecting U.S. investors and firms with local knowledge, commercial partners, and management.For Washington, the objective should therefore be to strengthen the conditions under which private investment can occur, rather than to substitute public capital for private investment. U.S. technical assistance can support tax-administration modernization and digitization; engagement through U.S. financial and regulatory institutions can contribute to deeper and more accessible capital markets; and commercial diplomacy can connect U.S. financial institutions and diaspora networks with firms and regulators in South Asia. However, these efforts should complement domestic institutional and structural reforms. Foreign investment cannot, by itself, create the governance or regulatory capacity needed to sustain a conducive environment for foreign investment.South Asia’s U.S. Investment GapHome to two nuclear powers, strategic geographical positioning, fast-growing economies, and a burgeoning young workforce, South Asia carries immense geopolitical and geoeconomic weight on the global stage. Yet, for all its strategic and economic potential, the region remains a markedly underinvested destination for U.S. capital.Despite South Asia representing roughly 25% of the world’s population and accounting for more than 4% of the world’s nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP), the region made up less than 3% of U.S. Net Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) positions and less than 2.5% of U.S. Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) positions in 2024. Even compared to smaller regions, South Asia severely lags behind. Net FDI holdings of the United States in South Asia amount to roughly one-third of net FDI in South America or Central America, and about two-thirds of net FDI in the Middle East.This mismatch is significant because no other single economy combines the same scale of outward investment, deep capital markets, and currency dominance as the United States. As of early 2026, the United States alone held more than $43 trillion in foreign financial assets and was the world’s largest source of FDI in 2025. This indicates that ultimately, where U.S. capital chooses to flow and where it does not could fundamentally shape economic trajectories around the world.Additionally, investment ties create stakeholders, commercial interests, and economic exposure that can, in parallel, increase a country’s strategic relevance in U.S. policy circles. For policymakers representing constituencies with large South Asian American populations, deeper economic engagement can also create a direct connection between foreign economic policy and domestic constituency interests. Viewing South Asia as an economic partner alongside its geopolitical and security relevance for U.S. interests can help align constituency interests with longer-term strategic goals.To examine the scale and composition of U.S. direct and portfolio investments in South Asia, this paper focuses on three key regional economies: Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan. Together, they make up the bulk of the region’s burgeoning population and account for more than 95% of South Asia's nominal GDP.U.S. Foreign Investment in Bangladesh, India, and PakistanForeign Direct Investment (FDI)As defined by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), FDI is a cross-border investment in which an investor owns at least 10% of the voting power of a foreign enterprise, indicating a lasting interest and some influence over its management. FDI positions generally include both equity ownership and debt between affiliated companies. In effect, FDI reflects an investor's confidence in a specific enterprise. Between 2014 and 2024, the U.S. net FDI position in India rose from roughly $33 billion to nearly $60 billion (Figure 1.1); but Pakistan and Bangladesh remained far smaller destinations, as both stayed below $1 billion throughout the period and generally moved within a range of only a few hundred million dollars. Relative to overall economic output, U.S. net FDI was equivalent to approximately 1.56% of India's nominal GDP in 2024, compared with 0.07% in Pakistan and 0.10% in Bangladesh (Figure 1.2). India's U.S. net FDI position was approximately a hundred times larger than that of either country, despite its GDP being only around ten times that of Pakistan and eight times that of Bangladesh.Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI)As defined by the World Bank, FPI consists of cross-border holdings of equity and debt securities—such as company shares or government- and business-issued bonds—that do not meet the 10% threshold for direct investment. Normally, it gives the investor no meaningful control over the issuing company.Foreign participation in the capital market can increase liquidity and give businesses and governments access to a broader pool of financing. For South Asian economies, it can also bring foreign currency to finance imports, service external debt, and manage balance-of-payments pressures. Unlike FDI, however, portfolio capital can be withdrawn quickly, making it less stable. In effect, FPI reflects confidence in the broader market infrastructure—the exchanges, regulators, and custodians—that make holding and trading those securities reliable. Figures 2.1 and 2.2 show a widening divide in U.S. portfolio investment across the three economies. U.S. portfolio holdings in India increased from roughly $130 billion in 2014 to nearly $400 billion in 2024. Relative to this significant rise, Pakistan’s position was much smaller and more volatile, declining from about $2.9 billion to approximately $1.4 billion over the same period. Bangladesh began below $1 billion at around $600 million, and fell sharply after 2017, reaching little more than $100 million by 2024. The gap in U.S. portfolio investment positions is even more pronounced when looking at the numbers relative to GDP. In 2024, U.S. portfolio investment was equivalent to approximately 10.3% of India's nominal GDP, compared with 0.38% in Pakistan and 0.02% in Bangladesh, illustrating the depth of India's capital markets relative to its regional peers.Because these figures measure positions rather than annual flows, changes may reflect new investment, divestment, company valuations, exchange-rate movements, or changes in security market prices.The Takeaway: Why the Above Statistics MatterThe metrics in the aforementioned figures reveal a widening divide within South Asia. While a broad mix of factors explains this divide, market participants and experts interviewed for this paper highlighted three enabling factors visible in India’s trajectory, relative to its regional peers:Growth in a formalized, digitized economy that renders domestic firms transparent to regulators and investors alike.Deep, liquid capital markets capable of absorbing institutional scale.An influential diaspora that reduces the barriers to entry.The following sections will examine each of these three core themes in detail, drawing actionable lessons from India’s relative progress, outlining how targeted reforms across formalization, capital market infrastructure, and diaspora engagement can help narrow the U.S. investment gap in South Asia.Taxation, Formalization, and DigitizationIn February 2026, the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires in Islamabad Natalie Baker wrote to Pakistan’s Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb about tax and customs disputes faced by PepsiCo. The company is not a small foreign entrant struggling to understand the system, as it is one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies and has operated in Pakistan as a textbook example of FDI since 1967. Thus, a company of such stature seeking its embassy’s intervention reflects a symptom of deeper dysfunction.Although this particular case was in Pakistan, its relevance also extends to neighboring economies.South Asia’s economic informality challenge is a trap and an obstacle for international businesses to sustain operations. At its core, economic informality refers to firms, workers, and commercial transactions that operate outside official registration, state regulation, and the tax net. One current cross-country series places informal output at roughly 26.7% of GDP in India, 33.5% in Pakistan, and 28.3% in Bangladesh. As of 2020, the World Bank estimates more than 80% of all South Asia's workers engage in informal activities, and over 90% of the region's businesses are informal. That also means a vast number of workers and firms remain outside taxation, social protection, access to financing, and reliable commercial datasets.Because governments cannot tax much of the economy, they impose higher rates and focus aggressive enforcement on businesses already visible to the authorities, such as PepsiCo. That raises the cost of complying and encourages smaller firms to remain undocumented. In turn, compliant companies are left competing against businesses that under report sales, avoid taxes, and ignore regulatory costs—a dynamic the World Bank identifies as creating unfair competition for formal firms.The macroeconomic consequence is evident in the region’s depressed fiscal capacity. While tax rates are often comparatively high, collections remain weak. The World Bank estimates that countries in the region collect between one and seven percentage points of GDP less than what their existing tax structures should generate. Bangladesh’s tax revenue fell to 6.9% of GDP in fiscal year 2025—compared to an average of 24% among emerging markets and developing economies (EMDE)—while Pakistan’s narrow base collection has repeatedly contributed to deficits, debt accumulation, and shortages of funding for infrastructure and human capital. Even India, while outperforming its regional peers with an overall tax-to-GDP ratio of 20.5%, lags behind broader EMDE benchmarks of 24%.The answer is not only to lower taxes but to also make compliance easier and ensure that a broader share of the economy participates in the tax system. It is to consolidate overlapping taxes, reduce arbitrary withholding provisions, limit exemptions enjoyed by politically powerful sectors, simplify filing, and create graduated regimes through which small firms can enter the system without immediately facing the same obligations as large corporations. The objective is to create a formal ecosystem where tax registration is worthwhile for businesses and continued evasion progressively harder.Digitization makes that balance possible by connecting individuals and businesses to tax records, bank accounts, licenses, property, and public services. Electronic invoicing can document transactions without relying solely on intrusive inspections. Automated customs systems can reduce discretion at ports. Interoperable payments create transaction histories that allow small firms to demonstrate revenue, access credit, and gradually become visible to the state. E-filing also lowers the time and cost of compliance while limiting face-to-face interactions that can create opportunities for corruption.India offers a good regional example for digitization. Aadhaar bank-account expansion, the Goods and Services Tax (GST) Network, and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) all connect identity, payments, taxation, and finance. The IMF estimates that GST revenue has increased by more than half a percentage point of GDP since 2018, accompanied by a sustained broadening of the noncorporate tax base. UPI recorded more than 240 billion transactions in FY 2025–26, while newer IMF research finds that Indian states that automated tax filing, permits, inspections, dispute resolution, and other administrative processes experienced higher microenterprise productivity. India also reduced its base corporate tax rate in September 2019 from 30% to 22% for eligible domestic companies, with a lower rate of 15% for eligible new manufacturing firms. Foreign fund managers credited the move with easing broader concerns about the Indian economy. The move was intended to strengthen India’s competitiveness in attracting investment, particularly against lower-tax Asian economies such as Vietnam and Indonesia.Beyond standard diplomatic advocacy on behalf of U.S. corporations, Washington can utilize several concrete policy channels to accelerate the region’s shift towards a more formalized economy and digitized tax base. The U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Technical Assistance can partner directly with the region’s finance ministries to modernize tax administration. Encouraging more American venture capital flows into South Asia’s fintech sector can accelerate this push across sectors of the economies. Additionally, impact investment frameworks can be structured to reward businesses that formalize, while strict enforcement against informal networks can channel an increase in diaspora remittances into banking rails. While ensuring that assistance remains strictly contingent on complementary reforms, Washington could also leverage its influence within international financial institutions to expand fiscal space for regional governments to reduce taxes in an effort to formalize.For direct investors, broadening the tax base generates the fiscal room needed to reduce high nominal corporate tax rates, directly incentivizing incoming FDI through a more competitive rate structure. At the same time, formalization levels the playing field by eliminating the unfair advantages enjoyed by unencumbered informal competitors, offering foreign firms a level operating environment. For portfolio investors, formalization significantly expands the pool of domestic firms capable of meeting international disclosure standards, raising institutional finance, and eventually listing on public stock exchanges. Stronger, broader tax bases could also stabilize sovereign balance sheets, reduce default risks, and lower country risk premiums across regional bond markets.Deepening Capital Markets Disaggregating South Asia’s portfolio investment numbers by asset type in Figure 3 reveals a fundamental structural divide in how U.S. capital engages with the region. U.S. holdings in India are overwhelmingly equity-driven, expanding from $121.7 billion in 2014 to $372.9 billion by 2024. By contrast, U.S. portfolio debt in India, while growing from $7.4 billion to $15.3 billion over the same period, remains a small fraction of total exposure.This heavy concentration in equity reflects foreign investor confidence in the long-term earnings growth and private sector dynamism of Indian corporations. But the confidence alone does not explain the heavy concentration in equities, as India caps foreign portfolio debt inflows in the single digits to mid-teens as a share of outstanding stock—a regulatory ceiling considerably tighter than anything applied to equity.In Pakistan and Bangladesh, the trajectory has been one of contraction. Equity holdings in Pakistan collapsed from a peak of nearly $2.8 billion in 2017 to just $346 million by 2024. Crucially, holdings of Pakistani debt securities eventually came to exceed equity holdings, signaling a shift where international capital seeks safer short-term returns rather than risk exposure in productive domestic firms. In Bangladesh, equity positions dropped from $859 million in 2017 to $109 million in 2024, while U.S. debt holdings evaporated entirely.The divergence in portfolio equity investment within the economies, as seen in Figure 3 and Figure 2.1 earlier, stems from market accessibility, liquidity, and scale. Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) classifies India as an emerging market, placing it within benchmark-tracking mandates that manage trillions of dollars globally, whereas Pakistan and Bangladesh remain classified as frontier markets. Pakistan’s 2021 downgrade back to frontier status followed shrinking market capitalization and trading volume, accelerated by capital flight during its placement on the Financial Action Task Force’s gray list after 2018. In Bangladesh, MSCI concluded that accessibility had been compromised by setting administrative floor prices, stopping share prices from adjusting freely to supply and demand, which halted market-clearing transactions and prevented foreign exits. The removal of the floor prices was welcomed in MSCI’s 2026 review, but MSCI warned that reinstating them could prompt consideration of a downgrade to Standalone status, which would lead to their exclusion from frontier market indexes and cause significant capital flight.For the index categorizations, India built the commercial and regulatory ecosystem required to execute trades at scale. Decades of institutional development under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) listed nearly 11,700 registered foreign portfolio investors, almost 5,000 equity brokers, 18 custodians, and 61 mutual funds. More importantly, this bridge is reinforced by a substantial American presence on the ground with firms operating in India such as JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and BlackRock.Simultaneously, India developed a domestic buffer against global market volatility through its Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) framework. By mobilizing automated, recurring household contributions, annual SIP inflows reached approximately $36.5 billion (₹349,589 crore) in FY2026. This domestic retail base allowed domestic institutional investors to make net equity purchases of $95.8 billion in FY2026, easily absorbing a record $19.6 billion withdrawn by foreign portfolio investors during the period.As of August 2026, at a market capitalization of roughly $5 trillion, India's exchanges operate at a scale that not only accommodates substantial institutional investment but gives Indian and multinational firms alike a credible domestic venue to raise capital through public market offerings. Pakistan's and Bangladesh's thinner exchanges cannot yet offer the same scale, with market capitalizations of roughly $71.5 billion and $28.3 billion, respectively, as of August 2026.Washington can directly accelerate this financial deepening by transferring institutional knowledge and mobilizing private capital. Through the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and its international training programs, technical assistance can help regional regulators meet global institutional requirements. In tandem, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) can act as an essential first mover and set a trend for commercial institutional investors to follow, especially as the Trump administration seeks a bigger role for the agency. For Bangladesh in particular, where the DFC is currently barred from operating due to statutory labor rights concerns, addressing these labor standards represents an entirely untapped opportunity for the Corporation’s investment.For foreign direct investors, the goal for economies like Pakistan and Bangladesh is to build lucrative capital markets with enough liquidity that foreign multinational corporations become keen to establish joint ventures with domestic firms and list those enterprises locally. For foreign portfolio investors, those public listings would create high-quality opportunities to purchase equity stakes. Building such an ecosystem—aligning the incentives of long-term direct investment, domestic industry, and international institutional capital—could transform regional securities exchanges into vital engines of national growth.Leveraging the Diaspora Networks in the United StatesSouth Asia already has commercial networks inside the United States. Within domestic conversations, these networks are discussed as a source of remittances. The more important investment role of the South Asian diaspora in the United States, however, is informational.Existing financial links between the diaspora and their countries of origin show the scale of opportunity. In 2024, the United States was the source of approximately $27.7 billion in remittances to India, $3.53 billion to Pakistan, and $2.96 billion to Bangladesh. Remittances are not FDI or FPI; they primarily support households and consumption. But they demonstrate that cross-border payment relationships, accumulated savings, and most importantly, connections between migrants and their home country already exist.Naturally, India possesses a considerable advantage. Pew Research Center’s estimates show that all three countries possess diaspora communities with substantial professional reach and financial capacity. In 2023, approximately 4.9 million people in the United States identified as Indian, compared with 580,000 Pakistanis and 270,000 Bangladeshis. Among adults aged 25 and older, 77% of Indian Americans held at least a bachelor’s degree, compared with 59% of Pakistani Americans and 51% of Bangladeshi Americans. Median household incomes were $151,200, $108,100, and $78,400, respectively.Beata S. Javorcik et al’s research in the Journal of Development Economics finds that migrant networks are positively associated with FDI in the migrants’ countries of origin, with an even stronger relationship among migrants who have received tertiary education. Separately, cross-country research by David Leblang finds diaspora networks associated with both direct and portfolio investment, where high-skilled diaspora professionals act as structural intermediaries. An executive or fund manager who understands both American business practices and local domestic realities can conduct informal due diligence, identify trustworthy partners, navigate bureaucratic hurdles, recruit local management, and introduce domestic companies to U.S. firms. These professionals help bridge the U.S. and South Asian investment ecosystems—including investors, financial institutions, and firms on the U.S. side, and South Asian financial markets, companies, and business networks—connecting the institutions and actors through which cross-border investment takes place.American financial institutions can help turn organic diaspora connections into institutional-grade investment channels. U.S. banks, asset managers, and fintech platforms already serving South Asian American communities can develop structured products, from dedicated country funds and diaspora bonds to venture platforms co-invested with local partners. U.S. commercial diplomacy can anchor this effort by aligning financial firms, diaspora networks, and regional regulators to clear long-standing friction around market access, capital repatriation, and legal protections.For foreign direct investment, a connected diaspora provides U.S. multinationals and venture funds with the market intelligence and operational leadership needed to de-risk entry. For portfolio flows, these structural bridges elevate fragmented retail savings into deeper, long-term holdings in regional public equities and corporate debt.How This Could Be Meaningful for the United StatesThe commercial case of investing in the economies of Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan comes first. South Asian markets could offer high-return opportunities for U.S. capital, even if performance varies across countries and market cycles. In fact, India’s stock market index, the NIFTY 50, significantly outperformed the S&P 500 in dollar terms over the five years from 2019 to 2024, and Pakistan’s KSE-100 delivered a roughly 87% return in U.S. dollar terms during 2024, more than triple the S&P 500's return. As shown in Figure 4, while Bangladesh's dollar returns lagged, Indian and Pakistani equities generated substantial cumulative gains in dollar terms between 2014 and 2025. However, for Washington, the case for an increased investment is not limited to the returns available to U.S. investors. Investment can also advance broader American interests, economic statecraft, and supply chain strategy. With the U.S. Congress expanding the DFC’s investing cap to $205 billion, the agency possesses enhanced tools—including debt, equity, and political risk insurance—to secure critical minerals, energy infrastructure, and vulnerable supply chains. Washington is already deploying this framework through targeted vehicles like the $500 million U.S.-Africa Strategic Investment Program to mobilize private capital. South Asia is the next logical frontier.Pakistan’s geological potential offers a channel for mineral diversification. The United States is already moving to develop this opportunity, with the U.S. financing to support critical-minerals development in Pakistan and the U.S. Strategic Metals (USSM) signing a memorandum of understanding with Pakistan’s Frontier Works Organization. Both key developments could further strengthen bilateral relations and help Pakistan capitalize on its critical minerals potential, which reportedly stands at “trillions” of dollars.India is becoming a practical component of the U.S. supply chain diversification strategy. Apple has accelerated iPhone production in India to reduce its reliance on China, while Micron opened a $2.75 billion semiconductor assembly and test facility in Gujarat in 2026. Boeing, meanwhile, sources more than $1.25 billion annually from a network of more than 300 Indian suppliers. These investments illustrate how India has fast emerged as an important partner and major regional player for the U.S. “China+1” and friendshoring objectives by building alternative manufacturing capacity in electronics, semiconductors, and aerospace, reducing exposure to concentrated East Asian supply chains.Bangladesh’s established manufacturing base provides a strong platform for supply-chain diversification. Its ready-made garment sector accounts for roughly 80% of total exports. Efforts to expand into leather, footwear, plastics, and light engineering aim to integrate Bangladesh deeper into global value chains as U.S. buyers diversify, with orders shifting from countries like China.There is, however, another case to be made for deeper U.S. investment in the region. Pakistan’s fiscal trajectory illustrates why long-term private investment is far more sustainable than repeated emergency stabilization. Islamabad’s request for a $10 billion U.S. Exchange Stabilization Facility to shore up foreign reserves and support its currency reflects Pakistan’s chronic reliance on emergency backstops. Having entered 25 separate IMF arrangements, Pakistan continually leans on international stabilization mechanisms where the United States serves as the largest shareholder, holding a 16.49% voting share. Bangladesh faced a similar episode after the COVID-19 pandemic and the shock from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine; when its current-account deficit widened, the taka depreciated, and foreign-exchange reserves fell. Its 2023 IMF program provided roughly $3.3 billion through the Extended Credit/Extended Fund Facility and another $1.4 billion through the Resilience and Sustainability FacilityWhile emergency bailouts prevent immediate sovereign collapse, they yield no lasting gains in export capacity, tax revenue, or industrial productivity. U.S. investment in minerals, energy, technology, and manufacturing can help build reserves, preventing balance-of-payments crises and the recurring financial and diplomatic liabilities for Washington. For the United States, this makes investment a more durable complement to stabilization than just providing emergency support.Finally, expanded commercial ties carry domestic importance for U.S. policymakers. More than six million Americans trace their origins to India, Pakistan, or Bangladesh, representing an influential, highly educated constituency with active professional bridges across the region. By engaging South Asia as a dynamic economic partner, rather than viewing it purely through a geopolitical and security lens, U.S. policymakers can also align domestic constituency interests with long-term strategic goals.Regional Investment Prospects Need a Sturdy FoundationThe three themes examined in this paper—a more formalized and digitized economy, deeper capital markets, and stronger diaspora engagement—are not the only factors behind the U.S. investment gap in South Asia. They are not shortcuts around the need for fundamental governance and structural reforms. South Asia’s foreign investment prospects depend on a much sturdier foundation that would involve a broader set of policy reforms that eventually make investments viable.Recent governance metrics underscore both India’s relative advantage and the region’s unfinished work. For foreign investors, stronger rule of law can reduce legal and political risks. In the 2025 World Justice Project Rule of Law Index, India ranked 86th of 143 economies, compared with 125th for Bangladesh and 130th for Pakistan, making it a relatively less risky investment destination. For U.S. investors in particular, corruption risks also carry potential compliance exposure under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA). Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index placed India 91st of 182 countries, Pakistan 136th, and Bangladesh 150th.Worldwide Governance Indicators tell a similar story. Although growing and yet to realize its full potential, India consistently outperforms its regional neighbors across government effectiveness, regulatory quality, rule of law, and, most importantly, political stability. The same institutional and regulatory vulnerabilities are repeatedly highlighted in the U.S. State Department investment climate reports for Pakistan and Bangladesh.There are no shortcuts to creating an environment conducive to greater investments. From Pakistan’s underdeveloped mineral wealth and Bangladesh’s manufacturing base to India’s expanding role in electronics, semiconductor, and aerospace supply chains, the region’s investment gap is not a shortage of opportunity. South Asia already possesses the demographic scale, entrepreneurial talent, and market opportunities required for global competitiveness.Investment policy in South Asia has often emphasized attracting foreign capital, while giving insufficient attention to the domestic investment environment that makes economies attractive to both domestic and foreign investors. Foreign investment follows domestic investment. Evidence from the works of economists Marc Lautier and François Moreau show that domestic investment is a strong catalyst for FDI in developing countries. They believe this implies that investment promotion policies towards domestic firms will be efficient in attracting foreign investment. It is important to note that U.S. policy and foreign investment cannot manufacture the institutional trust that only sustained domestic reform, and the domestic investment that follows, can produce.

About the Author

Ismail Faisal is a junior at UCLA, double majoring in Economics and Political Science, and from Islamabad, Pakistan. On campus, Ismail serves on the boards of the Pakistani Students Association and Bruin Reserve Bank. He has worked as an Analyst at Pakistan’s Ministry of Planning and Development. Ismail served as the 2026 American Pakistan Foundation-Asia Society Policy Institute Fellow.
